A fixed-effects Poisson or negative binomial regression for counts

Source: R/policy_evaluation.R
plnpois.Rd

The effect of a policy on counts (stops, arrests, offences) with unit and period fixed effects, reported as an incidence rate ratio, with cluster-robust standard errors that do not need the counts to be Poisson.

Usage

plnpois(
  data,
  unit,
  time,
  y,
  trtd,
  covs = NULL,
  offset = NULL,
  cl = NULL,
  family = c("poisson", "negbin"),
  conflvl = 0.95
)

Arguments

data

A data frame, one row per unit and period.

unit, time, y

Column names: the unit, the period (numeric, for example a year or a month index) and the outcome.

trtd

Column name of the treatment indicator (0 or 1).

covs

Optional column names of time-varying controls.

offset

Optional column name of the log exposure (for example log population).

cl

Column name of the clusters (default the unit), or two column names for two-way clustering (Cameron, Gelbach and Miller 2011): \(V_a + V_b - V_{ab}\), each term with the small-sample factor of the dimension with fewer clusters, and t on its \(G - 1\) degrees of freedom. A composite cluster (district by month, say) is one column made with interaction().

family

"poisson" (default) or "negbin" (NB2, \(Var(Y) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta\), with \(\theta\) by maximum likelihood).

conflvl

Confidence level (default 0.95).

Value

A data frame of class rmbl_fe_poisson, one row per term: term, estimate (log scale), se, rateratio, lower, upper (of the rate ratio), p_value; attributes n, drounits, clusters, family, theta (Inf for the Poisson).

Details

The model is \(E(Y_{it}) = \exp(\beta T_{it} + X_{it}'\gamma + \delta_i + \mu_t)\) (times the exposure, with offset its log), fitted by maximum likelihood. Units whose counts are all zero carry no information about \(\beta\) and are dropped first, as are periods with no count anywhere. The Poisson likelihood with fixed effects is consistent for \(\beta\) whatever the dispersion (Wooldridge 1999); the variance is the cluster-robust sandwich, with the small-sample factors of plndid. The rate ratio is \(e^{\beta}\), with interval \(e^{\hat\beta \pm z\,se}\).

With family = "negbin" the variance is \(\mu + \mu^2/\theta\): the fit alternates iteratively reweighted least squares at fixed \(\theta\) with the maximum of the profile likelihood in \(\theta\), and the sandwich uses the negative binomial scores with \(\theta\) held at its estimate (as sandwich::vcovCL() does for MASS::glm.nb(); fixest::fenegbin(), which treats \(\theta\) as a parameter of the variance too, gives slightly larger errors). With unit dummies this is the unconditional fixed-effects negative binomial, which behaves well as the number of periods grows (Allison and Waterman 2002); with few periods per unit prefer the Poisson, which is consistent whatever the dispersion.

References

Wooldridge JM (1999). Distribution-free estimation of some nonlinear panel data models. Journal of Econometrics 90(1):77-97. doi:10.1016/S0304-4076(98)00033-5

Santos Silva JMC, Tenreyro S (2006). The log of gravity. Review of Economics and Statistics 88(4):641-658. doi:10.1162/rest.88.4.641

Allison PD, Waterman RP (2002). Fixed-effects negative binomial regression models. Sociological Methodology 32:247-265. doi:10.1111/1467-9531.00117

Examples

p <- polex()
plnpois(p, "district", "month", "crimes", "reformed", offset = "logpop")
#>      term  estimate         se rateratio     lower     upper      p_value
#> 1 treated -0.092146 0.02220761  0.911972 0.8731289 0.9525431 3.334947e-05

# these counts are not overdispersed, so the negative binomial collapses
# to the Poisson fit and says so
plnpois(p, "district", "month", "crimes", "reformed", offset = "logpop",
           family = "negbin")
#> Warning: no overdispersion: theta is at its bound, the Poisson model fits
#>      term    estimate         se rateratio     lower    upper      p_value
#> 1 treated -0.09214602 0.02220756  0.911972 0.8731289 0.952543 3.334802e-05
